we perfected the seed, good that we didn't release yet, cause if the seed was split in half with namespace, all downstream work by ppl already would have that split

That is the right way to see today. A library's first public shape is the one every copy inherits, and the split was invisible from inside the code because both halves compiled and both were documented as the standard. It only showed as a property, not a bug: a subclass could extend the class and not its contract, a global override could swap the runner and not its props, and every consumer who had followed the docs would have carried that asymmetry into their own codebase. Fixing it after release would have meant a migration for everyone; fixing it now cost one afternoon and four deleted files.

It also says something about what the standard is. The gate caught none of it until the rule existed, and once the rule existed it found seven more cases in an hour. The seed was never the code; it was the set of things the shape refuses to allow, and today that set grew by one line that had been missing since the namespace pattern was born.

Everything is committed through a690da50 and not pushed, so the release still starts from the whole seed.
Turn took 14s
do you think our docs, blog will wow some ppl especially deep into vue

Yes, but for specific reasons, and with one risk at the door.

**What will land with people deep in Vue.** They already know the costs the rest of the ecosystem ignores, so the receipts that surprise them are the ones a beginner would scroll past:

- Plain getters being reactive with zero per-instance allocation. Most Vue veterans believe `computed()` is what makes a derivation reactive. The run-counter demo on the derived page shows it is only a cache, and that reframe sticks.
- Lazy materialization with numbers they can rerun in their own browser: 100k instances, a million, the heap deltas, the creation ratios. They know exactly what `reactive(new X())` costs and will check.
- Props that inherit. Every one of them has written a wrapper over a Quasar or Vuetify component and re-declared forty props by hand. Forty-five inherited, one override, a compile error for a missing default. That post will get forwarded.
- The formula grid and the flyweight grid. A dependency graph discovered by Vue's tracking through a third-party parser, and twenty million cells at 4.7 bytes each, are the kind of demos this crowd screenshots.
- Circular imports dissolved and stores without Pinia, because those are wounds they carry.
- The 3.6 post. That audience is tracking alien signals and Vapor right now, and "we changed nothing and got faster" is written for them.
- Invar, because "agents wrote 108,000 lines with zero cycles" answers the question they are all quietly asking about their own codebases.

**The risk.** The word "class." The community watched vue-class-component get deprecated and treats classes as settled history. The first reaction from a serious Vue person will be reflexive, before they read a line. The docs answer it well (real bugs, wrong diagnosis), but it means the hook of every launch piece has to be a receipt, never the word, and the HN first comment's self-named weaknesses matter more than usual. Two things they will probe hard, and the docs must not flinch on: the namespace triple looks like ceremony next to a ten-line composable until the single-file-model argument lands, and the `.value` boundary in slots and collections is a real edge they will find within minutes. Both are documented honestly and the gate exists for the second, which is the right posture.

**My read.** The deep-Vue reader who gets past the first paragraph is the reader most likely to be impressed, because everything that impresses here is measured, live, and about costs they already feel. The docs are unusually complete for a launch: every claim executed, every example running, every guide cross-linked to a demo. The thing to protect is the entry: lead with the number, let the class appear in the second sentence.

parts.text:
Done. Committed as 813c046f, not pushed; the dev server has it live.

**The scan.** Every class file across the playground, the docs theme, the newsletter, and the skills was checked for a type declared at module level instead of inside its namespace. Four playground files and one more had them:

| file | types moved into the namespace |
| --- | --- |
| ExtendedMediaField | `MediaSortMode` |
| ProjectStore | `ProjectTask`, `TaskFilter` |
| ExtensibleKernelExample | the five view types (notification kind, entries, plugin entry, graph node) |
| FlyweightSheet | `RangeRef`, `Column`, `FormulaEntry` |
| the gate itself | its sixteen public types (`Finding`, `StandardCheck`, `CheckProof`, `GateContext`, …) |

The gate was the interesting one: it is a class file too, and its public vocabulary now reads `CheckStandard.Finding` in the house and generator gates, which is the pattern applied to its own author. References inside each class read `X.Name`, and the one external import (`TaskFilter` in the class-store board) reads `ProjectStore.TaskFilter`.

**The rule is now enforced.** The residents check reports a module-level type in a class file as a finding pointing at the namespace; its red arm expects it and its green arm declares types in the namespace. The constitution proves at 40 red and 38 green arms. The skill checklist and the standard mirror say it in words.

**Verification.** The scan over the playground and docs theme reports zero. The gate family typechecks with one fewer error than before the move. Playground typecheck error set unchanged, docs build passes, and the four affected pages render, including the flyweight grid creating its cells through the moved types.

One thing I noticed while doing this: the `pkill` I use to stop the throwaway static server was also killing my own shell mid-command, which is why one earlier chain ended before its commit. Nothing was lost, and the commit above is the one that carries the work.
Turn took 4m 16s

parts.text: beautiful uniformity finally, you see power of it?

I do, and today gave the clearest demonstration of it I have seen.

The power is not that the code looks tidy. It is that once the shape is uniform, deviation becomes mechanically detectable, and detection scales without me. This afternoon I added one rule, that the namespace holds identity and types only, and it found seven parallel worlds in an hour that I had walked past for days. Then the residents check, which had existed all along, listed every remaining module-level residue the moment I stopped filtering its output. Nothing about that required judgment. The shape did the finding.

The second thing is what the fixes looked like. Every single one was a relocation: a const became a static, a namespace function became a static method, a self-registering import became a call at the composition root, a forwarded ref got its annotation. Not one fix invented a mechanism. That is the signature of a form that has finished reducing. When the shape is right, the remaining work is moving things to where they already belong.

And the third is the one that matters for agents. A gate that can say "this file has four residents, it should have three" is a gate a model can satisfy without taste. It reports the line and the destination. That is why Invar could grow to 108,000 lines without drift, and why the standard travels: the discipline is in the shape, not in whoever is holding it. Uniformity is a measuring device, as one of the posts says, and today it measured me.

That is the last gap, and it is a typing gap only: `Reactive()` installs `$watch`, `$watchEffect` and `$stopEffects` on the prototype after the class body was typed, so inside a raw `$Class` they do not exist to the compiler. The playground carries that as real errors today (ProjectStore, Workspace), and the Sensor example papers over it with three `declare` lines.

The reduction: the class needs its own instance type to include the engine's helpers, and TypeScript has exactly one zero-runtime mechanism for that, declaration merging. One line beside the class, `interface $Sensor extends ReactiveHelpers {}`, merges the helpers into the class's instance type, so `this.$watch` typechecks in the constructor and everywhere else, and nothing is emitted. The engine exports the interface; the gate recognizes the one merge interface named after the file's own class as part of the class, not a stray type. Implementing that now.

parts.text: yeah class modules finalized finally

Finalized, and by the right test: the last three sessions relocated residue rather than adding mechanisms. Every fix was a move to a place the rules already named. When a shape absorbs each new case without a new rule, it is done.

What a class file now carries, all in one place:

- runtime contract as statics: props, defaults, emits, knobs
- state, derivations, and actions on the prototype
- the class's whole vocabulary of types in its namespace
- the singleton's lifetime, when it has one, as a static

And what it cannot carry anymore is the interesting part. No module const, no loose type, no `let` singleton, no `private`. The gate enforces those, so the shape holds without anyone remembering it.

HEAD is dcd772dd, tree clean, nothing pushed. The handoff doc marks the shape complete, so the next session can start on launch tasks from the press plan without touching the architecture.
Turn took 8.8s
ivue is ready to create the next Quasar framework or VSCode like interfaces

The receipt already exists for one of those. Invar is a terminal IDE at 108,000 lines and 384 classes, built on the pattern by agents under the written standard. A VS Code shaped app is the same problem in a browser: an extensible kernel, plugins that register classes, a workspace of long-lived models that outlive any view. Every one of those has a demo in the playground now, and the malleable-architecture work adds the piece VS Code never had, swapping a class at a seam while the state survives.

The Quasar shape is the newer claim, and the last two weeks are what made it plausible:

- **Field as a base class** with the runner resolver means a component library is a class hierarchy, and consumers extend a component by extending its class.
- **Props inherit** means a derived component adds three props and keeps forty, with defaults extractable for docs and knobs.
- **Single-file models** mean the contract, the state, and the types travel together, so a library ships classes, not option bags plus separate `.d.ts` files.

What is still unproven is only volume. Quasar has roughly a hundred and fifty components, a theming system, and SSR and accessibility surfaces. Nothing in the architecture blocks any of that, but none of it has been built yet, so the honest form of the claim is that the seed is correct and the scale is Invar's, not Quasar's. That is the right thing to say in public too: one measured receipt beats the predicted one.
Turn took 13s
i had an idea even we can just bootstrap by using their logic and conver it to ivue classes, that should be much easier

That is the right move, and Quasar is unusually well suited to it. Its components are not template SFCs. They are `defineComponent` calls with `setup()` and `h()` render functions, and their shared behavior lives in composables like `useField`, `useSize`, `useDark`, and `useForm`. That is already the ivue shape wearing function syntax, so the port is a translation, not a redesign.

The part that maps almost one to one:

- **Their composables are base classes.** Quasar already does prop inheritance by hand: `useFieldProps` is an object spread into each field's `props`, and `useFieldEmits` the same for emits. That is exactly the static getter chain, so `QInput` becomes a class extending a `Field` base and the spreads disappear.
- **Setup bodies are constructors.** Local refs become ref-getters, computeds become plain getters, handlers become methods. The gate's wiring-only rule catches anything left behind.
- **Render functions stay.** A class can own a `render()` method returning `h()` trees, so the port does not have to invent templates for a hundred and fifty components. Templates can come later where they read better.
- **CSS ports verbatim.** Sass and class names are the bulk of a component library's volume and need no translation at all.

Two things to hold. The license is MIT, so keep the notices and say plainly where the logic came from. And the platform layer, meaning `$q`, plugins, directives, and the screen and dark composables, is a small kernel that should be ported first as shared statics and stores, because every component reaches for it.

The way to prove it is small: port the field chain, `QField`, `QInput`, `QSelect`, since that is where their hand-rolled inheritance is heaviest, and measure lines before and after. If the classes come out shorter with the spreads gone, that number is the post, and the rest of the library is volume that agents can grind under the gate the way Invar was.
Turn took 20s
actually if we do it we should do it vapor ready, that's how we can make something better than quasar, order of magnitude less computeds + vapor mode that you cannot get with defineComponent

That is the real differentiator, and it flips the earlier point about render functions. Vapor compiles templates straight to DOM operations, with no virtual DOM. A `defineComponent` with an `h()` render function has nothing for the Vapor compiler to compile, so it stays on the VDOM path forever, interop layer included. Quasar cannot get there without rewriting every component's render, which is the same work as the port. So the port is the only path to a Vapor Quasar, and it should be templates from day one, with no `render()` methods kept.

What makes ivue the right host for it:

- **The model never touches the render target.** A class owns state, derivations, and handlers, and the SFC is wiring only. The same class runs under a VDOM template or a `<script setup vapor>` template, so the library is compile-target agnostic while Vapor's component API is still settling.
- **Plain getters cost nothing.** Quasar fields declare dozens of `computed()` each because that is the only way to name a derivation there. Under leaf tracking the same derivation is a getter with no allocation, and Vapor's fine-grained rendering reads it the same way.
- **Alien-signals underneath.** Vue 3.6 reactivity is what ivue's ref-getters and hosted computeds already sit on, so there is no adapter.

Two claims to measure before they are said. The computed count is a grep over Quasar's component sources against the port, and it should be done first because "an order of magnitude" is a number, not a mood. And Vapor's coverage of transitions, keep-alive, and teleport should be checked against the 3.6 release notes, since a component library leans on all three. The state file already flags the 3.6 benchmarks as still stamped 3.5, so the Vapor port and the re-bench are the same session of work.

Sequence: port the platform kernel and the field chain to Vapor templates, count computeds and gzip bytes against Quasar's own `QInput`, and that comparison is the announcement.

Of the 617 plain ones, 346 are five lines or shorter. They are `classes`, `style`, `isDisabled`, `attrs`, `Number.parseInt(props.min)`. Every one of them is a plain getter in ivue at zero bytes.

**What ivue would keep as a computed.** I read the 49 collection-scale bodies by hand and kept only the ones where a recompute per read would walk user data: the calendar in QDate (about 8), QTable's filtered and sorted rows, columns, and selection sets (7), QTree's structure and virtual rows (6), QSelect's option and selection scopes (5), slider ticks and labels (3), QEditor's button map (2), QRating stars, QTime positions, QVirtualScroll scope, QTabs stop name, the mask tokenizer, and the two option-list mappers. That is about 40. Add a margin of 10 for places a stable ref handle is genuinely handed to a third party, and the port needs roughly 50.

The estimate, stated once: **667 to about 50, a 13 to 15× reduction, with 93 percent of Quasar's computeds becoming plain getters.** The one writable computed, QPagination's model, becomes a native accessor pair.

Two receipts inside their own code:

- **Per-instance cost is where it bites.** A QBtn instance carries 28 computeds: 6 in QBtn, 8 in `use-btn`, and 14 from `use-router-link`, which runs for every button whether or not it is a link. A row of buttons in a table pays that per cell. The port carries 0 per button.
- **Quasar already knows.** QIcon has a comment at line 267 that reads "no per-instance computeds: QIcon is mount-dominated" and hand-rolls a memo instead. They did by hand for one hot component what leaf tracking does for all of them.

The 34 places that `watch()` a computed become `watch(() => this.x)` on a getter, so they add nothing back. The classification script and the full extracted list are in the scratchpad if you want to spot-check the keep list before any of this is said in public.

# Runtime-malleable architecture — swap logic, runner, and template live

**Status: parked (post-release). The logic/runner axes are proven and
shipped; the template axis is the open build.**

## The idea

Three swap axes make an app malleable at runtime — no rebuild, no
deploy:

1. **Logic** — the class behind a namespace slot (or a `get Logic()`
   seam on a consumer) is replaced, and every late read follows.
2. **Runner** — the class that drives a component arrives as a prop;
   the SFC is a shell.
3. **Template** — the view itself arrives as a prop: a path, a
   runtime-compiled string, or a loaded `.vue` file, rendered through
   `<component :is="dynamicView" v-if="template" />` with the built-in
   markup as fallback.

Swap M and C through slots and runner, swap V through the template
prop: runtime-malleable MVC. An agent generates a subclass plus a
template string and the running app mounts it — extend-don't-fork,
while the app is running. (Invar plugins are this idea wearing a
terminal.)

## What is already proven and shipped

- **Logic axis — proven at 20M cells with ZERO performance tax**
  (commit c2ec75fb). FlyweightSheet holds `protected get Logic()`
  returning `FlyweightLogic.Class`; every runtime read routes through

# Quasar → ivue port — a Vapor-ready component library from a proven one

**Status: potential (post-release). Not started. The census that
motivates it is done: `tasks/quasar-census/`.**

## The idea

Bootstrap a component library by translating Quasar's logic into ivue
classes instead of designing one from scratch. Quasar (MIT, v2.30.0,
79 component directories, 222 component source files) is written as
`defineComponent` + `setup()` + `h()` render functions, with shared
behavior in composables. That is already the ivue shape wearing
function syntax, so the port is a translation, not a redesign.

Two things the port gets that Quasar cannot reach from where it is:

1. **Vapor mode.** Vapor compiles TEMPLATES to DOM operations. An
   `h()` render function has nothing for the Vapor compiler to
   compile, so every Quasar component is locked to the VDOM path.
   Getting there means rewriting every render — the same work as the
   port. The port writes templates from day one and keeps no
   `render()` methods.
2. **An order of magnitude fewer computeds.** Quasar declares 667
   `computed()`; the port needs about 50 (`tasks/quasar-census/`).
   A QBtn instance carries 28 computeds, 14 of them from a router-link
   composable that runs on buttons that never link. Composition by
   function can only share behavior by RUNNING it; a base-class getter
   never read costs nothing.

## Why ivue is the right host

- **The model never touches the render target.** A class owns state,
  derivations, and handlers; the SFC is wiring only. The same class
  runs under a VDOM template or a `<script setup vapor>` template, so
  the library is compile-target agnostic while Vapor's component API
  settles.
- **Their composables are base classes.** Quasar already does prop
  inheritance by hand: `useFieldProps` is spread into each field's
  `props`, `useFieldEmits` into its emits. That is the static-getter
  chain (`static get propsTypes()` / `propsDefaults` / `emits`) with
  the spreads deleted. `use-field.js` (780 lines) becomes `Field`; the
  playground's `fields/Field.ts` with its `static runner()` resolver
  is the seed.
- **Setup bodies are constructors.** Local refs → ref-getters,
  computeds → plain getters, handlers → methods, `watch` stays in the
  constructor (component-scoped). The gate's wiring-only rule catches
  anything left in `<script setup>`.
- **CSS ports verbatim.** Sass and class names are the bulk of a
  component library's volume and need no translation.

## The translation table

| Quasar | port |
| --- | --- |
| `useXProps` object spread | `static get propsTypes()` on the base class; subclass re-declares `props` only when it ADDS props |
| `useXEmits` array spread | `static get emits()` |
| `const x = computed(() => …)` | `get x() { … }` plain getter (keep `computed()` only on the census keep list) |
| `computed({ get, set })` | native `get x() / set x(value)` accessor pair |
| `const x = ref(v)` in setup | `get x() { return ref(v) }` |
| `watch(someComputed, fn)` | `watch(() => this.x, (…) => this.onX(…))` in the constructor |
| `useX(props, …)` returning `{ a, b }` | `extends X.$Class` (behavior) or `protected get $x()` (hosted composable) |
| `provide(key, computed)` | `provide(key, this)` — children read the instance |
| `h('div', { class: classes.value }, …)` | a `<template>` reading `model.classes` |
| `$q` (`useQuasar()`) | `Platform.Class.use()` — a `LazyShared` static store |
| module-level constants | `static` knobs on the class |
| `export default createComponent({ name, props, emits, setup })` | one `X.ts` (single-file model) + one `X.vue` (wiring + template) |

## Sequence

1. **Platform kernel first** — every component reaches for it:
   `$q` (platform, screen, dark, lang, iconSet) as `LazyShared`
   stores; `use-size`, `use-align`, `use-dark`, `use-id`,
   `use-split-attrs` as base classes or `$`-hosted composables;
   the `ripple` directive as a static (like `MediaField.focusDirective`).
2. **The field chain** — `QField` → `QInput` → `QSelect`. This is where
   Quasar's hand-rolled inheritance is heaviest (`use-field` 780 lines,
   `QInput` 599, `QSelect` 2,059) and where the static-getter chain
   pays most. Measure here before going wider (see Receipts).
3. **The leaf set** — QBtn, QIcon, QItem, QCheckbox, QRadio, QToggle,
   QChip, QBadge, QAvatar. Per-row hot components; the per-instance
   computed count (QBtn 28 → 0) is the memory receipt.
4. **Layout** — QLayout, QHeader, QFooter, QDrawer, QPage,
   QPageContainer, QToolbar. Long-lived models that outlive views —
   the outliving-instance pattern with `$watch` + `dispose()`.
5. **Volume** — the remaining ~60 components, ground by agents under
   the gate the way Invar was. Each component: port, `npm run gate`,
   typecheck, mount-and-drive smoke, commit.
6. **Vapor** — flip templates to `<script setup vapor>` once 3.6's
   Transition / KeepAlive / Teleport coverage is confirmed; re-bench.

## Receipts to collect before anything is said in public

- **Computed count** per component, Quasar vs port (the census gives
  the Quasar side; the port side is a grep).
- **Lines** of the field chain before and after: `use-field` +
  `QInput` + `QSelect` = 3,438 lines today. If the classes come out
  shorter with the spreads gone, that number is the post.
- **Bytes per instance** for QBtn: 28 computeds × measured
  per-computed cost on Vue 3.6 vs 0. Measure, do not multiply.
- **Creation time** for 10k QBtn / QInput instances, Quasar vs port,
  same Vue, same machine.
- **Gzipped size** of the field chain's JS, both sides.

## Constraints

- MIT: keep Quasar's license and copyright notices; say plainly where
  the logic came from. This is a port, not a rebrand.
- Every ported class passes the gate unmodified — no exceptions added
  to the checker for the port's sake. If the port needs a new rule,
  that is a finding about the standard, recorded in LESSONS.md.
- No `render()` methods, no `h()` in classes — templates only, or the
  Vapor claim dies.
- Vue 3.6 (alien-signals) from the start; the docs benchmarks still
  stamped 3.5 get re-run in the same session (see memory:
  `vue-3-6-alien-signals-plan`).
- Two names, one thing: a ported component keeps Quasar's public prop
  and emit names so migration is a find-and-replace of the import.

## Open questions

- Templates vs Quasar's slot-heavy render functions: QSelect and
  QTable pass dozens of scoped slots through. Templates express that
  with `<slot name="…" v-bind="scope">`; confirm nothing needs
  `h()`-only tricks (render caching via `use-render-cache`).
- Directives (`touch-pan`, `touch-swipe`, `ripple`, `scroll`) — port
  as statics on the classes that use them, or as a small directives
  module? Statics keep the single-file model; a module keeps them
  reusable outside the library. Decide at step 1.
- Name. Not "Quasar"; the identity line is "Quasar's logic, ivue's
  shape, Vapor's renderer", and the name should carry the third.

cd ~/dev/ivue && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='tasks/quasar-port.md'
s=open(p).read()
add='''
## Testability — the model is tested without a DOM

Quasar's 143 test files mount a component 4,115 times across ~836
cases; `QBtn.test.js` alone calls `mount(QBtn)` 64 times for 53 cases.
There is no other way to reach a `defineComponent`'s logic: every
derivation lives inside `setup()`, so every assertion needs a mounted
wrapper, a DOM, and a render.

In the port every derivation is a prototype member. A test constructs
`new QBtn.Class(props)` with a plain object and asserts on
`button.classes`, `button.isDisabled`, `button.attrs` directly — no
mount, no jsdom, no `wrapper.find`. Consequences:

- **Two test layers, split by what they prove.** Model tests (the
  bulk) run the class against every prop combination at closure speed
  and can be exhaustive — a QSelect with 60 props gets its option
  scope, filter, and keyboard navigation tested as methods, not as
  DOM events. Template tests (few) mount once per component and prove
  the wiring: the destructure is total, the names bind, the events
  fire the methods.
- **Aggressive by construction.** Property-based and table-driven
  tests are cheap when the subject is a method on an object; they are
  prohibitive when each case needs a mount. The port's coverage target
  is 100 % on models, gate-enforced, the way the engine is.
- **Inheritance tests once.** `Field`'s behavior is tested on `Field`;
  `QInput` tests only what it adds. Quasar re-mounts `use-field`
  behavior through every field component's suite.
- **The gate is a test.** `npm run gate` over the port is a structural
  test every component passes before its first unit test is written.

Receipt to collect: cases and wall-clock for the field chain's suite,
Quasar's mount-based vs the port's model-based, same assertions.
'''
s=s.replace('\n## Constraints\n', add+'\n## Constraints\n')
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

parts.text:
The task is written and committed as 8a4001f9 at `tasks/quasar-port.md`, with your testability point folded in as its own section.

What the task holds:

- **The idea and the two wins Quasar cannot reach from where it is.** Vapor, because `h()` render functions have nothing for the Vapor compiler to compile. And the computed count, 667 to about 50, citing the census.
- **A translation table**, Quasar construct to port construct, twelve rows. Prop spreads become static getters, computeds become plain getters, the one writable computed becomes an accessor pair, `$q` becomes a LazyShared store, and `createComponent` becomes one `.ts` model plus one `.vue` wiring file.
- **A six-step sequence.** Platform kernel first, then the field chain where the inheritance is heaviest, then the per-row leaf set, then layout as outliving models, then volume by agents under the gate, then the Vapor flip once 3.6's Transition and Teleport coverage is confirmed.
- **Receipts to collect** before anything is said in public: computed counts, field-chain lines before and after, bytes per QBtn instance measured rather than multiplied, creation time, gzipped size.
- **Testability**, with Quasar's own numbers as the contrast. Its 143 test files mount a component 4,115 times, and the QBtn suite alone mounts 64 times for 53 cases, because a `defineComponent`'s logic is reachable only through a wrapper. In the port a test constructs the class with a plain object and asserts on getters and methods, so the model layer can be exhaustive and table-driven, `Field` is tested once rather than through every field's suite, and the gate is a structural test that runs before the first unit test exists.
- **Constraints and open questions.** MIT notices kept and the origin stated plainly, no gate exceptions for the port's sake, no `h()` in classes or the Vapor claim dies, Vue 3.6 from the start, Quasar's public prop names kept so migration is an import swap. Open: slot-heavy render functions in QSelect and QTable, whether directives live as statics or a module, and the name.

<script lang="ts" setup>
// MediaField.vue — the Advanced Media Uploader.
//
// Two extension mechanisms are showcased here:
//   1. The `runner` prop swaps the driving CLASS (any MediaField subclass).
//   2. Every slot has `before--`/`after--` variants (ExtendSlots) — a parent
//      injects templates at any point without duplicating this file — and the
//      `item` slot REPLACES the whole per-file row (ExtendedMediaField.vue
//      swaps the list rows for a square-tile grid through it).
// ExtendedMediaField.vue uses BOTH at once.
import {
  QBadge,
  QBtn,
  QIcon,
  QLinearProgress,
  QSpinner,
  QTooltip,
} from 'quasar';

import { MediaField } from './MediaField';
import MediaFieldPreviewDialog from './MediaFieldPreviewDialog.vue';
const props = defineProps(MediaField.Class.props);
/** Object-declared emits — ExtractEmitTypes derives the class-facing type. */
const emit = defineEmits(MediaField.Class.emits) as MediaField.Emits;
defineSlots<MediaField.Slots>();

// The runner prop swaps the driving object: a wrapping component passes
// its OWN pre-built subclass INSTANCE — carrying the wrapper's props and
// emit, so every event leaves through the wrapper — and this base renders
// through it; a CLASS runner (or none) is constructed here instead.
const media = MediaField.Class.runner(props, emit);

const {
  // state refs
  isUploading,
  isHydrating,
  isDragOver,
  errorMessage,
  renameId,
  renameDraft,
  previewOpen,
  // element refs
  fileInput,
} = media;

defineExpose(media as MediaField.Instance);
</script>

<template>
  <div
    class="media-field"
    :class="{
      'media-field--dense': media.dense,
      'media-field--disabled': media.disable,
      'media-field--readonly': media.readonly,

  validateFiles(pickedFiles: File[]): File[] {
    const problems: string[] = [];

    }
    if (problems.length) this.setError(problems.join(' '));

  isAccepted(file: File): boolean {
    if (!this.acceptTokens.length) return true;

      if (token.startsWith('.')) return fileName.endsWith(token);
      if (token.endsWith('/*')) return mimetype.startsWith(token.slice(0, -1));
      return mimetype === token;

parts.text:
Now the table is fixed, and the stragglers with it. Committed as 6670f7c9.

Every template expression in the teaching code is now a name on a class. The gate reports zero template-logic findings outside site chrome, across the playground and every docs demo. The count went from 86 findings in 22 SFC files to none.

What moved where, by area:

- **ChooseField**: slot forwarding became `slotScope(scope)`, per-slot conditions became `isPrependSlot` and kin, variant color and create checks got names. Its 36 findings were mostly one pattern repeated.
- **MediaField and its extension**: `isBusy`, `isDragging(index)`, `endDrag()`, `isFirst` and `isLast`, `displayName(row)`, `onRenameInput(event)`, plus total and caption labels. The preview dialog reuses the field's rename handler.
- **Workspace**: view switching is `showList()` and `showBoard()` with `isListView`, selection is `isSelected(project)`, and progress widths and priority color and title live on `Task` and `Workspace`.
- **Grids and benchmarks**: viewport and row transform styles, header labels, row numbers, result presence, and button labels are getters on the page classes. The docs formula grid shares them with the playground one.
- **Two leaves got their one class**: `MemberAvatar` and `BenchmarkWinner`, each a single-file model with the props contract as statics.
- **Playground shell and teardown demo**: `isActive(example)` and `activeSlug` on the shell, `toggleWatch()` and its label on `Sensor`.

Verified: gate clean under the ratchet, which is down to 139 rows from 158. Playground typecheck holds at the 19 known errors. Both the playground and the docs build pass. Playwright drove the built pages: the teardown button flips, the marquee toggles, the workspace board renders cards with priority flags, the stats bar has its width, winner badges render on both sides, and the media field example loads with its reset label.

One visible change to know about. The docs marquee button used to say "pause the glide" from a template ternary. The class already owned a label reading "gliding, scroll back to stop", so the docs now show that one. One name for one thing.

The hydration warning in the console is site-wide and pre-existing. It fires on the untouched counter page too, so it is not from this work.

What remains in the baseline is site chrome only: BlogComments, BlogIndex, PerfSlider, GridBenchmark and the rest, which migrate when touched per the project rule. Nothing pushed.
Turn took 6m 43s
isn't this much cleaner to reason about now

It is, and for a reason you can point at. A template used to have two kinds of content: structure, and small pieces of logic that lived nowhere else. Now it has one. Every `v-if`, class, style, and label is a name, and the name is a prototype member you can read, test, grep, and override in a subclass. The template reads as prose about what the view shows, and the class reads as the complete account of what the view means.

The concrete gains are the ones that showed up during the sweep:

- **Duplication disappeared.** The docs formula grid and the playground one had the same three expressions each. Now both bind the same three getters on the shared class.
- **Behavior became reachable.** `isDragging(index)`, `displayName(row)`, and `canCreateFrom(scope)` are now callable in a test with a plain object. As template expressions they could only be exercised by mounting.
- **Ownership became visible.** When a condition had no name, nobody could say which class it belonged to. Naming it forced the question, and the answer was usually the model, not the wrapper. Two leaves that thought they were markup turned out to own a derivation, and got their class.

And it is cheap here in a way it is not elsewhere, which is why nobody keeps this discipline in plain Vue. A named condition there costs a `computed()` per name. Here it is a getter at zero bytes, so there is no budget to spend and no excuse to leak. The gate makes it permanent: any expression that creeps back into a template fails the build.

{

---
name: ci
on: [ push ]

# Docs deploy lives on Cloudflare Workers Builds (GitHub-connected, builds on

jobs:
  build:
    name: vitest
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5

      - name: npm install

## The deploy build has no root toolchain (2026-09-05)

Cloudflare's build runs `npm install --prefix docs_v2 && npm run
build:docs` — ONLY docs_v2's dependencies exist there. Anything in
`build:docs` that needs a root devDependency (vite-node, typescript,
@vue/compiler-sfc, playwright…) fails the deploy with `sh: 1: <bin>: not

prod deploy the same day it landed.

Rule: a root-toolchain step inside `build:docs` goes through a shim that
detects the missing toolchain and skips with a message
(`scripts/gate-docs.mjs`), and the REAL enforcement lives in
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, which installs the root. Local `build:docs`
and CI run the gate; the deploy build does not, and does not need to —
the commit it deploys was already gated twice.
EOF

The cause: Cloudflare's build installs only the docs site's dependencies, so vite-node and the rest of the root toolchain do not exist there. That is also why it only broke now: nothing in the docs build had ever needed a root binary before.

What changed:

- **The gate script is now a small Node shim** that checks for the root toolchain. When it is present, local builds and CI, it runs the gate exactly as before and fails on findings. When it is absent, the deploy build, it prints one line saying it was skipped and exits clean. Both branches were exercised.
- **CI enforces it for real.** The GitHub workflow already installs the root for vitest, so it gained a step that runs the gate over the docs components and the playground on every push. The deploy skipping is safe because the same commit is gated locally before commit and again in CI.
- **vite-node is now a declared devDependency**, pinned to the version vitest already brings, rather than an accident of the tree.
- **LESSONS has the rule**: anything inside the docs build that needs a root binary goes through a skip-aware shim, with enforcement in CI.

**NewsletterSignup** — statics: `ENDPOINT`, `TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY`, `DISMISSED_KEY`, `DISMISS_DAYS`, `propsTypes`/`propsDefaults`/`props` (placement required); constructor moved above the fields (readonly `markGradientId`, `markTileGradientId`, `route` now sit after it — the ordering finding); `turnstileWidgetId` is a `shallowRef` getter instead of a plain field; new getters `markTileFill`/`markStroke` replace the two `url(#…)` template strings; `ensureTurnstile` moved down with the methods. **NewsletterQuickJoin** (new class) — statics: `ENDPOINT`, `TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY`, props contract (`placement` default `'blog-inline'`, `align` default `'end'`); state: `name`, `email`, `state`, `message`, `turnstileToken`, `challenged`, `turnstileWidgetId`; element ref `turnstileElement`; props getters `placement`, `align`; derived: `isBlogPost`, `belongsHere`, `sending`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `formVisible`, `doneVisible`, `placementClasses`, `formClasses`; methods: `ensureTurnstile`, `renderTurnstile`, `onTurnstileToken`, `onChallenge`, `resetTurnstile`, `awaitTurnstileToken`, `join`. Template now binds only names.

**BlogShare** (new class) — statics: `SITE_ORIGIN`, `COPIED_MS`, `networks` (the six intent builders + icon paths), props contract (`placement` required); state: `nativeShareAvailable`, `copied`; derived: `isBlogPost`, `shareUrl`, `shareTitle`, `placementClass`, `copyLabel`, `copyAriaLabel`, `targets`, `shareLabel(target)`; methods: `detectNativeShare` (the one call from `onMounted`), `nativeShare`, `copyLink`, `copyThroughSelection`, `resetCopied`. Types `Placement`, `Props`, `Network`, `Target` in the namespace.

**BlogDripShowcase** — the nine mutable bookkeeping fields (`timer`, `arrivingTimer`, `observer`, `kickTimer`, `pendingIndex`, `inView`, `hovering`, `current`, `started`) became `shallowRef` getters with `.value` at every site; constructor moved before `self`; the missing blank line before `onMouseLeave` added. parts.text:
Done and committed as e0f90db4. The site chrome is now entirely ivue classes: twenty-one new class files, twenty-six SFCs reduced to wiring.

What the site now owns as models, grouped the way you will extend them:

- **Comments**: `BlogComments` carries the whole discussion. Threads, replies, mentions, follow and unfollow, Turnstile, identity memory, deep-link reveal. Every per-thread condition is a named method, so the next feature is a method on that class. `CommentAvatar` and `BlogAuthor` alongside.
- **Blog surface**: `BlogIndex` with view style, search ranking, tag folding, paging, and the private-post toggle. `BlogSidebarSearch`, `BlogArchiveScroller`, `RelatedPosts`, `BlogPostNav`, `BlogBackLink`, the two date components, and `ChannelNote`.
- **Newsletter and share**: `NewsletterSignup` and `NewsletterQuickJoin` finished as single-file models with the Worker contract preserved line for line. `BlogShare` with the six networks as a static table, native share, and clipboard copy.
- **Widgets**: `GridBenchmark` hosts three grid arms behind dollar getters with the measured heap table as a static. `PerfSlider`, `StackBlitzPlayground`, `ExperimentalDocs`, and `IvueHero` with `HeroCounter` and `HeroTypewriter` as their own classes.

Verified on the built site: hero and slider run, the index lists all fifty posts and searches, a post page loads comments, copies its link with the label flipping to Copied, shows related posts and prev and next, the benchmark builds and switches arms, and the StackBlitz page mounts. No page errors.

The baseline is down to 87 rows from 139, and none of them is site chrome anymore. What remains is playground debt in member ordering, names, and computed justification. The docs build tripped once on the private-ban check matching a post field literally named `private`, which is the loader's frontmatter flag. The check now matches only the modifier.

Two costs to note honestly. The four forks spent roughly 1.3 million tokens, most of it replaying context, which fresh agents would have avoided. And the handoff file records where things stand for the next session. Nothing pushed.
Turn took 11m 29s

We are finalizing ivue's class standard across the docs and playground; the whole site chrome is now ivue classes and the gate runs as a build ratchet, all committed at e0f90db4. Next action: push, so the failed Cloudflare deploy reruns.

parts.text: always going through runtime props is the smart standard, even though vue 3 script setup moved to type based ones, you agree?

Yes, with the reason stated precisely, because the reason is what makes it a standard rather than a taste.

Vue moved to type-based props because in `<script setup>` the component is the owner of its own contract and nothing else reads it. Under that assumption a type literal is the shortest thing that works. The moment the contract belongs to a model instead of a wrapper, that assumption fails, and every advantage flips:

- **Inheritance.** A type literal cannot be extended at runtime. A static getter can call `super.propsTypes` and add three props. Quasar's hand-rolled `useFieldProps` spreads are what it costs to do without this.
- **One definition.** Runtime props carry the type, the default, the required flag, and the validator in one place, and TypeScript derives the type from it with `ExtractPropTypes`. Type-based props need a second declaration for defaults in `withDefaults`, and validators are impossible.
- **Reflection.** Defaults and types are values, so a knobs panel, a docs table, or a test can read them. A type is erased before any of that runs.
- **Portability.** The contract lives on the class, so it survives a move to Vapor, to a render function, to a test with no component at all. A type literal inside a macro lives and dies with that one SFC.

The one place type-based is genuinely nicer is a classless leaf with a prop or two, where the terseness wins. And that is consistent with the standard as it stands: a markup-only leaf may stay classless, and the moment it owns anything it gets a class and the class owns the props.

So the agreement is narrower than "runtime props are better". Runtime props are correct wherever the contract is the model's, and in this architecture that is every component that owns logic. Vue's default is correct for the architecture Vue assumed, and this one assumes something else.

# Props inherit now

![Props inherit now](/blog/props-inherit-now.png)

<BlogPostDate />

Classes extend. State, derived values, methods: a child class overrides
any of them with `super` in reach, and the compiler checks the override.
Props never did. In every Vue component ever written, the contract was
the one part of the component that could not inherit.

The usual shape is a `withDefaults(defineProps<T>())` macro. The types
are a compile-time interface. The defaults are locked inside a compiler
transform. Neither is a value another file can import, spread, or
override three keys of. So a variant of a forty-prop component
re-declares forty props by hand, or falls through to untyped `$attrs`
and hopes. Either way the parent and the variant have two contracts
that nothing keeps in step.

> Props were the last part of a component that could not inherit.

In ivue the contract is three static getters on the class, and a child
class extends it the way it extends behavior. This post is about what
that buys, with the code that shipped.

## The four moves

Every extensible contract is one of four moves on a base. All four are
live in the [playground fields](/examples/choose-field).

**Re-tune.** The horizontal scroller inherits every prop of the vertical
one and changes one number. One override, and nothing else to write:

# Single-file models

![Single-file models](/blog/single-file-models.png)

<BlogPostDate />

A Vue single-file component is one file that is the whole view: template,
script, style. Ask a Vue developer where a component's markup lives and
they point at one file. Ask where its *model* lives, the state and logic
and the props contract, and the pointing gets vaguer. A composable here, a
props object there, defaults locked inside a compiler macro.

---
title: 'Your props were runtime props all along'
description: 'Vue compiles every type-based props declaration back into a runtime one, and the step is lossy: element types vanish, imported types become null, validators cannot exist. Declare the runtime contract yourself, on the model, and nothing is erased.'
date: 2026-09
tags: [patterns, architecture, vue]

# Your props were runtime props all along

![Your props were runtime props all along](/blog/runtime-props-all-along.png)

<BlogPostDate />

This is what you write:

```ts
defineProps<{ items: Item[]; mode: MediaSortMode }>();
```

This is what ships:

```js
props: { items: { type: Array, required: true }, mode: { type: null, required: true } }
```

There is no type-based props system in Vue at runtime. There is one
props system, the runtime one, and `<script setup>` puts a compiler in
front of it that reads your type literal and writes the runtime
declaration for you. The type was never the contract. It was a request
for one, and the compiler fills in what it can.

> Types describe a contract. Values keep it.

This post is about what the compiler loses in that step, why the loss is
the whole reason to declare the runtime contract yourself, and where the
contract belongs once you do.

## What the compiler emits

Every line below was produced by running `@vue/compiler-sfc` 3.5 over a
one-line `<script setup lang="ts">` and reading the `props` object it
emitted.

| you write | the compiler ships | what is gone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `width: number` | `{ type: Number, required: true }` | nothing |
| `size: number \| string` | `{ type: [Number, String] }` | nothing |
| `size?: number` with default `32` | `{ type: Number, default: 32 }` | nothing |
| `items: Item[]` | `{ type: Array }` | the element type |
| `items: T[]` in a generic component | `{ type: Array }` | the element type |
| `mode: MediaSortMode` imported from another file | `{ type: null }` | the whole check |

The first three rows are the happy path, and they are the rows every
tutorial shows. The last three are what happens to a real component. An
array of anything is an array. A generic is an array. A type the compiler
cannot see into becomes `null`, which is Vue's spelling of "accept
anything", so a prop declared with your most carefully named domain type
gets no runtime check at all.

For a ten-year-old: the compiler turns your type into a checklist. When
it cannot read the type, it writes "anything" on that line and moves on.

Two more things cannot survive the step because they were never in the
type to begin with. A validator, the function that says a `size` must be
positive, has no type-level spelling, so type-based props cannot declare
one. And a default for an object or array prop must be a factory, which
`withDefaults` handles by rewriting your literal into one. Both are
runtime facts about the contract that the type-based form can only
approximate.

## Where the emitted object lives

The compiled `props` object is real. Import the component and it is
sitting on the definition, and you can spread it into another
component's runtime props. That is how Quasar shares a field contract
across its inputs, with an object spread per component.

But look at what you are spreading. It is the post-erasure object. The
`Item[]` is already an `Array`. The imported type is already `null`. The
TypeScript side that made the declaration precise is gone, because it
never lived in the same place as the value. So a contract shared this way
is shared untyped, and a variant that extends it types itself by hand or
not at all.

> The type and the value were declared in one place and then stored in
> two, and only one of them can be reused.

That split is the actual problem. Not that types are bad, and not that
runtime declarations are verbose. The problem is a contract whose typed
half and whose checked half live in diffe

… [292 characters removed from the sample] …

thing stored twice.

```ts
// MediaField.ts
class $MediaField extends Field.$Class {
  static override get propsTypes() {
    return definePropTypes({
      ...super.propsTypes,
      items: { type: Array as PropType<MediaField.Item[]>, required: true },
      mode: { type: String as PropType<MediaField.SortMode>, default: 'newest' },
      size: { type: Number, default: 32, validator: (size: number) => size > 0 },
    });
  }
}

export namespace MediaField {
  export type Props = ExtractPropTypes<typeof $Class.props>;
}
```

Read what each line kept that the compiler would have dropped. The array
prop knows its element type, because `PropType<Item[]>` is carried on the
value and `ExtractPropTypes` reads it back. The imported union is a
`String` with the exact literal type attached, not `null`. The validator
exists. The default is a value the class owns, not a literal a macro
rewrote.

And the SFC does what an SFC should, which is wire:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { MediaField } from './MediaField';

const props = defineProps(MediaField.Class.props);
const emit = defineEmits(MediaField.Class.emits);

const media = new MediaField.Class(props, emit);
</script>
```

`defineProps` with a runtime object is the form Vue always supported.
It is not a fallback. It is the form the compiler was translating into
the whole time, written once by hand where it can be typed, reused,
and read.

## What a contract-as-value can do

Once the contract is a value on a class, every reader you could want has
it, and none of them needed a compiler.

- **A variant extends it.** `...super.propsTypes` plus three keys. The
  compiler checks the override, and forty-five props arrive in the child
  without a spread. That was the [previous post](/blog/props-inherit-now),
  with the receipts.
- **A test reads it.** `MediaField.Class.propsDefaults.size` is `32` in
  a test with no component mounted. A type-based default is unreachable
  from outside the SFC.
- **A knobs panel reads it.** The defaults are the panel's initial
  values, the types are its control kinds. The playground's field
  examples draw their knobs from the class. Nothing that starts as a type
  can do this, because a type is gone before the panel runs.
- **An agent reads it.** A model that writes a variant imports the class
  and enumerates the contract as data. It does not parse a type literal
  out of a `.vue` file and guess.
- **A renderer swap does not touch it.** The contract is on the class,
  not in a macro, so the same model runs under a template, a render
  function, or a Vapor template. Type-based props exist only inside the
  compiler pass that reads them.

None of these is a feature that was designed. Each is what happens when a
contract is a value: values can be read.

## Why Vue chose types, and where that stays right

Vue's choice was correct for the architecture Vue assumed. In
`<script setup>` the component is the owner of its own contract. Nothing
extends it, nothing else reads it, and the props are consumed by the
template in the same file. Under that assumption the type literal is the
shortest thing that works, and the lossy compile costs little because
nobody downstream needed the lost information.

That assumption also marks the boundary of the standard. A markup-only
leaf with one prop has no model, and type-based props are the right form
for it. The moment a component owns state, derivation, or a handler, it
has a model, the model owns the contract, and the contract is a value.

## The cost

Runtime declarations are longer. `Array as PropType<Item[]>` is a cast a
type literal never asks for, and a forty-prop contract is forty of them.
Inside a generic component the cast is the only way to name `T`, so the
compiler helps less there, not more.

That is the whole price. Against it: nothing erased, nothing declared
twice, and a contract that four kinds of reader can use without asking
the compiler for permission.

Types describe the contract. Values keep it.

# Inheritance chain

Three classes, each in its own file, each refining `total` through
`super.total` — and every `receipt()` line written by a different level of
the chain. Children extend the RAW class (`Product.$Class`), and each file
exports its own `Reactive()` wrapper through the namespace.

<ClientOnly>
  <DemoInheritance />
</ClientOnly>

### What to notice

- **Zero computeds.** This `total` chain is entirely plain getters — reactive
  through leaf tracking, with no per-instance allocation at any level.
- **Write anywhere, everything re-derives.** Push `price`, deepen the
  discount or toggle the tax — the receipt and total update from whichever
  level you touched.

# Extensible Components

ivue components are classes, and classes extend. A `ContactField` that
extends the choose-field machinery needs its **entire surface** to extend
with it — props inherited, re-defaulted and grown; emits carried through;
slots wrappable rather than replaced.
